utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. All the accused are here. Defence teams are full. Ms. Condon is back. Welcome. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. The witness is already in the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Are you ready to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just ready to go, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before you start, Madam Fauveau, last week you raised -- or not rather raised, you had sought admission of 5D173; and at a later stage, during the same sitting, an admission also of transcript pages 3378 to 3381 from the Oric case. We have had time to go through both your submissions during the previous sitting as well as the transcripts from Oric, from the Oric case. Our position is as follows: Unanimously, we decide not to admit the Oric case transcript pages 3378 to 3381. These were not put to the witness, and this is of course without prejudice, should you later on decide to pursue this matter through witnesses. As then as regards document 5D173, by majority judgement, Judge Prost dissenting, we have decided to admit the document. That closes the chapter on this document, and we can proceed with the testimony of Witness 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I also wish to thank those of you who filed the documents relating to the objections that you wish to bring forward to the intercepts. I thank you. We will be going through them, and we will come back to you as we go along. And the Prosecution, also, we thank you for your document on the estimated length of the Prosecution case. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we left off last Thursday, you had just told the Trial Chamber about some of the other buildings that had been struck by the shelling that had killed your six-month-old son. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, was anyone else killed or injured in that shelling attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other wounded in that area, and there was another woman who had been wounded earlier; and the second time when she was wounded, she died. So she was finished off in this second shelling. I don't know. I was busy in the area where I was, but perhaps there were some other instances that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, again, in this period in 1993, at some point while you were living in Srebrenica, did something happen to the water-supply? And if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, there was water when I came to Srebrenica. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, stop. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this line of questioning. What is -- why is it relevant what the conditions where is in 1992 and 1993 and what the situation was with water. This is outside of the time-frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two points, Your Honour. One, it is within the overall time period of the indictment, but specifically this is relevant to the conditions that prevailed in 1995 with respect to the water situation. I believe that the relevance of the witness's testimony will become clear, and we expect it to be linked up with other evidence concerning the situation of the water-supply as of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will consult with my colleagues. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, but please come to the point quickly, Mr. Thayer, because we want to make sure that it is within the relevance parameters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, would you just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what, if anything, happened with respect to the water-supply in 1993 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The water was cut off before the line of the enclave was formed, the Srebrenica enclave line. There was a reservoir in the free territory. But when the enclave line formed, the reservoir or the main source of supply remained outside of the enclave. I don't know if it was mined or closed, but in any case there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point in the spring of 1993, sir, did UNHCR trucks begin delivering humanitarian aid in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime maybe in January or February one convoy passed, but this was infrequent because humanitarian access was not permitted. There was a crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at the time that the convoys began arriving, did you make any efforts to get your family out of the enclave at that time? And if you did, would you just briefly describe how you did that or how you tried to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the -- the situation was terrible for different reasons, hunger, the danger of shelling, there was chaos and at one point I wanted to evacuate my family. It was allegedly said that the convoy would be safe. However, the chaotic situation that ensued in which people rushed to these trucks, I was afraid of -- that my small child that I was holding would be suffocated in the crowd; so then I gave up and returned, and that's why my family did not reach the Tuzla free territory. Should I say more?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's -- that's sufficient for now. Thank you, sir. And when you refer to trucks, are you referring to the empty aid trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Empty aid trucks that had brought in humanitarian aid. It was amongst the first or perhaps it was the first delivery of humanitarian aid. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point thereafter in the spring, sir, was there a shelling attack which stands out in your mind in which your daughter played some role in -- in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since a large number of people were living in the enclave, about 40.000 in this small area, then the children, the young people, organised a kind of tournament and at one point the shelling began. I happened to be in my house at the time, and I was going to eat. There was no water. I told my daughter to go and bring water. But then when the shelling began, I was afraid for her and I ran out in a panic and I ran to a small stream -- spring from which we brought water. And on the way I saw wounded people, the dead, and all of that, but I continued to run in a panic, calling out for my daughter. On the way on the road, I saw a child with a canister. It was lying on its stomach. I don't know if the child was dead, but it wasn't moving. And a woman a bit farther down was sitting, and she was immobile. She was leaning on some kind of fence or something along the road; then I went back home and I was calling out...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to stop you right there, sir. Is it fair to say you found your daughter safe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I called her and she responded, she said, "I'm here."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you help with the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later. Well, immediately I went back and there was a young man up there with a kind of small tractor, and we picked up the wounded and we took them to the hospital. The hospital was overcrowded and I was standing there, and a doctor came by. And since I had been once in that hospital when I was wounded, he asked me to help in dressing others' wounds. I started to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea from being there how many people were killed or were wounded in this shelling attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am really wondering where is the relevance with regard to this line of questioning by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There are two lines of relevance, Your Honour. Again, it goes to the state of mind of this witness. At the time he had to make decisions about whether he was going to leave the enclave of Zepa and whether he was going to put his family on a convoy to leave Zepa or whether they would remain in Zepa. It is relevant because it is corroborative of the testimony of a previous witness who had similar testimony, which I believe at the time was unique. I think it's important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I don't think you should be saying this in front of the witness. One moment. I need to consult with my colleagues. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do see the relevance, of course, but I think it's a long, winding road that you are taking. Perhaps you can simply put a simple, straightforward question to the witness: What was your state of mind at the time you decided to leave Zepa? That's all. Can you we take it up from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be happy to that, and I will try to move-- continue to try to move things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't take it as a criticism. We are not criticising your kind of examination-in-chief. In this trial, we are blessed with a very high quality of lawyers on both sides, which has been beneficial, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the Trial Chamber has heard a significant amount of testimony concerning the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica. Was there also an UNPROFOR presence in the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was there. In 1993, they were there at the same time when -- when the Srebrenica enclave was formed the Zepa protected area was also formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was the UNPROFOR base located in Zepa, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Zepa. I think it was in -- they were in premises in or near the elementary school in Zepa, in the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with those UNPROFOR soldiers, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did, I bought, I exchanged. I actually bought petrol from them in order to be able to use my motor saw, in order to be able to repair my fence. I was also constructing a small building to put the cows in, so that's when I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know what country these soldiers were from, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did humanitarian aid begin arriving with some regularity in the Zepa area between 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compared Zepa and Srebrenica, the humanitarian aid arrived quite regularly in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that you took part in distributing that aid in and around your father's village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I distributed the humanitarian aid in my father's village.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point in 1995, did something happen to the aid that had been coming to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a month before Zepa fell, and I'm not quite sure about the -- the time, the humanitarian aid was halted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did it stop all of a sudden or did it -- was it reduced over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reduced gradually over a period of time, but there were no major difficulties; but then it completely stopped about a month before, approximately a month before. I don't remember exactly which period, how long before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this period of time, sir, did people from Srebrenica begin arriving in your father's village? And if so, why were they going there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the enclave of Zepa had a lot of arable land, people sort of helped out by making or growing their own food and receiving humanitarian aid. So they were in a somewhat better situation than the people in Srebrenica. However, during the last two or three months, people kept arriving constantly. Practically, they were begging; they were asking for food from people from the Zepa enclave. They came to my father's village. Also, they came to me, people from Srebrenica, people who knew me and they were counting on my help. So I did help.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did something cause you to move your family yet again, this time from your father's village to another location in or about this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was intense shelling and a great deal of insecurity in the area where I lived, because some Chetnik check-points I was able to see from my window with the naked eye. I could see the artillery, the tanks, whatever it was. It was dangerous to remain in the village, so all of us moved out except for maybe about a dozen people, and we all moved into the woods in the mountains in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, if we move into private session for just one question and then...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, after Srebrenica fell, did you participate in any way in the defence of the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When there was this intense shelling and attacks on the lines, then I also took part. I was at the Stublic check-point; and when I was resting, I was actually monitoring the Drina canyon. I was monitoring it to see whether Chetniks would go through the canyon and enter the village and slaughter all the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, sir, were you close to a Serb position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time when I was at the line, it was very close, maybe 20 or 50 metres away. Chetniks were there. We could hear them. They were singing, and they were taunting us, saying all kinds of things: "We'll come to your village; we'll rape all your women; we will kill you; you will have to look at us as we do all that, you Balijas;" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, did you receive information, sir, that the women, children, and elderly would be taken out of Zepa? And if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother came back from the line and he asked me why I hadn't taken our families to Zepa, because he had heard that there would be an evacuation, that UNPROFOR would do that, or the Red Cross with the UNHCR; and then I said that I hadn't heard anything about that, because this village was a little bit further away from the other places. We did not get any information. So my brother and I, we took our families and we took them to Zepa, or rather to Stitkov Dol, which was the place where we'd left our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, sir, at the time you and your brother decided to take your families to Stitkov Dol, where were the Serb forces by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the lines, the defence lines in the Zepa territory had been broken through. The defences had been shattered. It was at night, and we saw a village opposite Stitkov Dol in the direction of Bosanica. We saw the that the village was already on fire. There was there huge fire there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the name of that village, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vratar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on your way to Stitkov Dol, sir, did you also encounter other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we -- actually, what happened is we caught up with them, and we overtook them as we moved towards Stitkov Dol. There were some elderly people, infirm. They couldn't move very fast. In Stitkov Dol, I found a lot the people, a large number of people. I don't know the exact number, but there were many people there. And I think that they were there in Stitkov Dol because they were afraid what the security situation was in Zepa because Vratar was not very far away from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber where -- and I'll show you a map at the end of your testimony and we'll go through some of these areas you have mentioned, but for the time being can you just describe where Stitkov Dol is in reference to Zepa, directionally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to the north of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you have said that there were many people at Stitkov Dol during the time you were there. Can you provide any estimate for the Trial Chamber how many people you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there may have been about a thousand people; women, children, the elderly. I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, sir, what was your state of mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a tense situation. I was afraid of what would happen to our families and to ourselves, to all of us who were already there. It was quite clear already that there was this disaster looming. It was dangerous because I had to leave my wife and children behind. I felt terrible. It was very difficult, and it was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you see what other people's emotional state was at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all faced the same situation, and we all had the same feelings. People were crying, the children were crying, women, I myself was crying. I couldn't say anything to my children when we parted. I just said to my wife, "Take care of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, by this time, sir, had you spoken to people from Srebrenica? Do you need a break, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we may just need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is very unfortunate when we have face distortion. We can follow less. [Microphone not activated] So we will have -- how much time -- witness, how much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of minutes, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will be out here; and as soon as the VW section have given him coffee or water or whatever and we are in a position to start again, let us know. But make sure you are feeling comfortable. And any time you need a break, we'll -- we'll give you one. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, by the time you arrived at Stitkov Dol, had you spoken to a man named Salko Mustafic and another man named Mujo Rustanovic about their experiences during the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk about that. When Srebrenica fell, they were in Srebrenica; and when it fell they, tried to reach the free territory but they couldn't get through. They doubled back, and they told me about all the terrible things they had been through; the fear, the journey. They told me about this place on the route to Kaldrmica, and there was a hill and there was a stream where there was an ambush. A tree fell down, there was an explosion, a lot of people were killed in that explosion, and then all of a sudden there was shooting from all over the place. They couldn't even tell where the shooting was coming from, and they survived by pure chance. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) media telling them that Zepa had fallen a long time ago and that Srebrenica itself would fall, that they should surrender. So they stayed at my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, I just ask would for a redaction at page 14, line 11. There is a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. Let's redact that. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, after leaving your family at Stitkov Dol, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left our family in Stitkov Dol, we went back home, or rather, to the house where I had been staying just before that. There were many people there, and it was our plan to stay there for a while, or rather not there, but to take shelter in the Drina canyon, because we figured that smaller groups of less than ten people could perhaps pass through the line or the siege line around the enclave because this had already been broken through. And I didn't even know where the lines were anymore, but we figured that smaller groups of up to ten people could pass through unnoticed. We took some food with us, we took the food to the Drina canyon, and we stashed it there in some holes in the rock so that it would be there for us when we decided that the time was right for us to move to the free territory. So I went back home from those rocks and krags to get some more flour, and en route I encountered a school mate of mine. He was with my cousin and some relatives of mine, and he told me he that wanted to move to Macedonia through Serbia. I asked him if I could join him, and he said no problem. But he said that before the war, before the occupation, he used to work in Partizan Put in Serbia, that he knew the route well and that it was possible to get to Macedonia undetected. That's why I decided to do so. I went back to the cave and I told my brothers, well, I decided to go. I think we should split because maybe some of us would survive; and if we all stuck together, then we would all be killed. So I went back to the Drina canyon. We crossed the Drina at Crni Potok. We used some rubber tubes that we had blown up to cross, and it was rainy. It was a rainy night; it was dark. We had to build a small fire on the other side to dry our clothes, and then we moved into Serbia. We climb up a mountain there, and up there we took off our dirty clothes. We changed into new clothes, because we figured that we would not be so conspicuous. And if a car came our way, we could perhaps pay the driver to take us down to Macedonia or wherever we could; but then one morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you right there, if I might. Let me just take you back just for a couple of follow-up questions. You mentioned being in a cave. Can you describe the terrain in which you were hiding, first of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cave was in the Drina River canyon. It was very close to Poljanice. It was called Sokolina. It's a cave that my father actually used in the Second World War to hide from the Chetniks. The name of the place is Tomodo, and there is a meadow up there. And there is a small foot path used by hunters, and it has a water spring. There is a water spring near the cave, and -- and below it were some -- was some rugged terrain, some rocks that were, in fact, unpassable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber who else was in this cave with you at the time you made the decision to try to head out for free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brothers; my cousins, Salko Mustafic, Mujo Rustanovic, Halid Osmanovic, about 50 people all told together with us. Those were all people that we knew, mostly people that we knew and; and later on more people gathered as my brother told me because groups were formed of about ten people, so that many people who did not join any of the groups didn't know what to do. And some people approached me because they knew that I knew some routes leading into the free territory, and perhaps they thought that I was capable of taking them all to the free territory. Yet what I did is I actually went the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In coming to your decision to head to free territory, did you consider any other alternatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I did consider -- this was a very difficult situation. There was this great deal of tension. It was psychologically very difficult. I was mulling over so many things. The first or second day, it was so difficult for me. You just don't what to do. You cannot go up in the heaven. You cannot go down into the ground. There was this great fear of being captured, of torture. And sometimes I really thought I really wanted to just commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the approximate date that you crossed the Drina? And if you don't remember the actual date, can you estimate for the Trial Chamber approximately how many days it was after you had left Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think maybe three or four days before I was captured. I left my family there. I think it was on the 25th. I think it was the 25th that I left my family; and then when I was captured, we had to put a date on the statement that they took from us, and I think that the date was the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to show you a map, and it is P02419.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is basically an extension of map 8 that was in your map book. The original map 8 is of limited use to us because we're talking about a region that's to the east, so we have furnished -- I believe you all have hard copies and hard copies have been distributed to Defence counsel. If I may ask the assistance of Madam Usher for the ELMO. I'm not confident that we are going get the degree of detail on e-court that we need, so I think we're going to have to resort to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to identify on this map some of the areas you have talked about. And, please, we are still in open session, so I just want you to point out on the map certain features which, if you can see them on the computer, great; if not, just work off the ELMO, please. Sir, can you take a look at the image that's on your screen; that may actually be more helpful. Can you read the locations that are on your screen? Are they legible to you, or do you need it look at the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You and I looked at this map a few days ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you identify certain locations that you have testified about today, and can you just review some of the locations that you see on that map just by name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stublic and Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have a better focusing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you could move the map a little up, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my father's village. Stitkov Dol and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll just make sure that we redact that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, sir, without referring to the specific nature of these areas, if you could just identify the names of some of these locations that are highlighted on the map. You just pointed out one location. Could you just state the names that you see on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can repeat the names. Zepa, Stitkov Dol, Poljanice, my father's village, and here on the other side, Stublic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just move the map so we can see Stitkov Dol in relation to Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It wasn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I didn't think we need to redact that. All right. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, based on having reviewed this map, is it a fair and accurate map from what you can see of the areas and territory as you recall it then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you could look at the screen because I'm going to ask you to mark one area on the map on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll up just a touch, please, on -- on the e-court map.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you if you could, with the continued help of Madam Usher, just mark the -- the location as best as you can tell on the map, where you crossed the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place is called Crni Potok; that's the location here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you could take that pen and just mark an X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I don't think where he is going to mark is at the moment visible on the ELMO. Oh, I see. He is doing it on e-court. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just write mark PW-155 anywhere on the map and then we can save it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today's date?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is 5 February.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And we can save it now. Now, sir, I believe you -- you just testified a few moments ago that you recall being captured on August 2nd. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you recall that date because it's the date you had to sign a statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the day when I was captured, when I was tortured, and statements were taken from us, personal information, and so on. We had to write the date. I think that he told us, that person sitting at the desk, he told us the date. I think he told us the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this was at a location called Sljivovica in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first statement was at a school that day, in a school. Before we came to the Sljivovica camp, we came to the camp in the night. We were transported to the Sljivovica camp during the night from that village. From the school, we were transported in trucks to a construction company where the camp was in Sljivovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, approximately, how long were you held in Sljivovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there about two days, according to my recollection. I thought I was going to be executed when I was called out; however, I and 450 other people were called out. And during the night, we were transferred to another camp called Mitrovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, is it fair to say in the time you were in Sljivovica, you were beaten and abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, Your Honours. I object to the relevancy of this testimony. He has now testified he is into Serbia. He is now talking about some mistreatment by Serbian soldiers, and it is absolutely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this? Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is relevant in two respects. One, it is one question to complete the picture of what this individual has gone through as he sits here before the Court today. I think that's relevant evidence. Again, it's one question, and then a similar question for the second location and I intend to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't attach any relevance to these events for the purpose of this case, Mr. Thayer. So please move to your next relevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when were you released from Mitrovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1996. And we were not allowed to go back to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were told that we shouldn't even think about it. They said we could go to a third country; and since we did fill in some forms, I did not put down my wish, which country I wanted to go to, but I just put down as soon as possible and as far as possible from here. And a family replied -- they applied to be my sponsor. It was a U.S. Family, and I left on the 22nd of January, 1996. I didn't go alone; there was a group of 112 or 120 people. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, sir, you were reunited with your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did your wife tell you about her experience being transported out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She did say that it was chaotic, that people were pushing, that it was difficult to get on to the convoy, and that the convoy that was there was a Chetnik convoy, and a people transport; that it was a long road to Tisce, where they were disembarked from the buses and the trucks, and they had to walk on foot for six or more kilometres in order to reach the free territory. She told me that in certain places they were stopped. They were checked or searched in some places - I don't know the names - to see if there were any militarily able -- or able-bodied men in the trucks and buses, and the children were scared. The children also experienced horrible situations when they were going from Tisce to the free territory, because on the way there were Chetniks asking for money, stopping people, searching some people. She said that people were disappearing along that way. For example, there was a cafe on the road, and people were going inside to drink water and they never returned. They disappeared there. She told me that since it was dark she said that she went to sit. She was carrying a little girl, and she was carrying some things and she was tired. She went to take a rest, and she thought that this was -- a tree stump on the road. And she wanted to sit there, but actually it was a dead body that was covered over by the road; and then she moved away, because she didn't want the children to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I just have a couple of final questions for you. Did you and your family leave Zepa freely, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. It was forcible departure. It was finishing up the ethnic cleansing. Zepa was a protected zone, and the Chetniks burned the surrounding villages and occupied the territory. There was no way that we could stay. I don't think that any of those people, the women who were transported, said anything about people asking them if they wanted to stay or not. There was no question of that. There were a lot of people who were killed. This was forcible transfer of those who had survived from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, why did you not stay with your wife and children at Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid for my life because all the able-bodied men, even children of age 14, were killed and taken off the convoy. There were 14-year-olds in the Rogatica camp, who looked older. I don't know. So it didn't even occur to me. It would be like suicide to stay and to go with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 8th of April, 1992, you left the town where you had been living until then. Can you just tell me how long you had lived in that town before the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1998 [as interpreted] until the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: From 1988 until the 8th of April, 1992. So it was from 1988 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps during the few months before your departure, were you able to notice that the situation was deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. There was a military group that arrived from Serbia to take the military documentation from the Bratunac municipality, and it was a bit chaotic because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. What I'm interested in is the following: You could conclude that also from the media and on the basis of the general situation there that the situation was deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In 1991, two young men were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you finished your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that before that, in Kravica, two young men were killed on the road, because even then those secret Chetnik, illegal Chetnik guards were formed. And there was a killing in Kragivoda as well, and the cleansing had started and the collection of people and there was an ambush; and on that occasion Bahrudin Osmanovic and another man, I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's not go into all of these details right now. I'm interested in something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic and Witness, you speak the same language and you're going too fast; particularly, Witness, you are not allowing a short interval of time, a small pause, short pause, after Mr. Zivanovic finishes his question, and that is creating difficulties for the interpreters. The same applies to you, Mr. Zivanovic. Please allow a short pause before you go on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is about when you left the town where you were. Did many other Muslims do the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even slightly before people were afraid. At the time it was already a little bit chaotic. People who were afraid, and it was chaotic and I...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that five days before that, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had issued a general call-up? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I didn't hear about that mobilisation, no. Well, maybe it was the Serbian self-declared authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1996, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say March 1996.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said a few days before your departure, or to be more specific it was the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not aware of that, no. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that that day, when you left, I think -- or the day before, the imminent danger of war was proclaimed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: People who left the town where you lived at the same time as you also didn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the imminent danger of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About the mobilisation and the imminent danger of war being declared.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sensed it when the Chetnik check-points were formed. When the police changed uniforms in my town, that's when I sensed the danger and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I didn't ask you about when you sensed what, but when you found out that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed a mobilisation or declared a mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never found about it. I never heard of it or found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Amongst the people who left the town where you lived, at the same time as you did, there were plenty of able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who left with me, my two or three brothers up in the village, yes, it's true, that there were a lot of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were also obliged to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was my duty even before, but people refused. They didn't want to because there was a war in Croatia at the time, and the army of Yugoslavia was taking those people to the front. I had a neighbour who escaped from Bihac who was supposed to go to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not asking you about the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down. I can sense the frustration in the interpreter's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the mobilisation by the former Yugoslav People's Army, and I'm not asking you about the mobilisation declared on the part of the army of Republika Srpska and the organs of Republika Srpska. I'm speaking quite specifically about the mobilisation declared by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You said that you didn't know anything about that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely didn't know anything about it. I didn't know that there was an army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In June 1992, you were at a check-point in a village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was being done at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were guarding; we were on guard duty. They were so-called village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. And were you able to do what you wanted at the check-point, or did you have any kind of instructions about what to do in specific situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group of people -- out of that group of people, we were all assigned to the -- a check-point at specific places or times. The guard duty went on for 24 hours, and we made our own roster of guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And my question, again, were you able to decide by yourselves what you were going to do at the check-point? I'm speaking about you personally, or you had some instructions from someone about what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that I belonged to, the village guard's group, we had Zuhrija. He was the head of the group or the commander of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he an able-bodied man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were all able-bodied, I presume. There were also some elderly men who were afraid that we would experience the same thing that had happened in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this person that you say was the commander of the group, was he perhaps an officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he belong to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Later he probably did, when it was organised as an army, as the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- were you authorised at the check-point to let soldiers of Republika Srpska or as you called them here, Chetniks, into the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we didn't dare let them in, because it was known that they wanted to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you would have stopped them with weapons, had they tried to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just a -- a -- an obstacle to finishing off all the people who had survived from Srebrenica and Bratunac. There were people left over who had managed to escape from Srebrenica, and they were afraid of what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your family did not leave the enclave when a considerable number of civilians left. Can you please tell me if there was any obstacle after that to your family's leaving the obstacle -- leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an obstacle; you just couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me if the Bosnian authorities permitted civilians to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know that. We were cut off, both in terms of the media and in every other way. We were isolated, and I don't know. As for that information, I don't believe hearing anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you need a permission from the BH authorities to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even if I could have gotten such an authorisation, where was I supposed to pass? I couldn't dig my way out under ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, in light of the fact that you lived for four years in the town where you lived before you left, I'm sure that you knew quite a few people of Serbian ethnic background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of my very good friends, my former good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if during the war any of those people from this town and from the surrounding area were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really keep in touch all that much, and I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but probably there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and we will have the break soon after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about two of your friends who tried to move into the free territory from Srebenica. You described the event involving the tree, the fallen tree. Did they tell you how they managed to get out of the situation? Or to be more precise, did they move through the woods all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hid during the day; and during the night, they moved through the woods and they would sneak up to the Muslim houses. For instance, in Babunica [phoen], they took some food there. They found some flour and were able to cook some food for them, and then they reached Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So there were some Muslim houses in those areas at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of them had been burned down. Some were still left standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they wanted to get into the Muslim houses specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they moved along the routes that were familiar to them. Those were not all Muslim villages, some of them were ethnically mixed villages. But those were places where they could move through unnoticed, because those villages had already been abandoned. People had been expelled from those villages, and the villages were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I have no more questions, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Witness, we are going to have a 25-minute break now, and we will reconvene soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I -- Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me, were you ever a soldier at any time from 1992 to the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could not really call that a soldier. These were just village guards in 1992, early 1992. When I was wounded, I no longer took part in the guards at all; and in the army later on when the enclave of Zepa fell, when all of us left to the lines, this was a voluntary effort because we were all afraid that the place we were in would also fall. So this is my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me then that in 1992, in Kamenica village and after that, you armed yourselves, you and your colleagues, with rifles and pistols, and there were roughly 400 of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the village guard in 1992. My question is: You were armed with hunting rifles and pistols and weapons of that nature, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I was a village guard in (redacted), and I had a hunting rifle that I used only while I was actually on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it would be safer just to be in private session for this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's very wise. Let's go into private session. Sorry for interrupting you like this, Mr. Meek, but I think we all anticipated what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, giving that statement and telling the Office of the Prosecutor, concerning the time period of approximately the end of June of 1992, that, "We started to organise village patrols when a certain village was burned down. We armed ourselves with hunting rifles and pistols." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having said this in those terms. I remember that I said that I was in village guards in (redacted), that we organised ourselves. We did not arm ourselves because when I got to the guard post, I found a hunting rifle there. It was handed over to me by my colleague who was leaving the guard post, so the rifle was there all the time. People would just hand it over to each other because there were -- there was not enough weapons. Those were hunting rifles, weapons that were legally owned, before the aggression started. Hunting rifles, pistols, things like that. And later on people would use some pipes to make some makeshift weapons, and that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we need to redact in line 8 of this page, the name of the village. Is that the reason why you were standing, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. I think you will find an earlier reference as well, which hasn't been redacted, to that village a few moments ago, just before we went into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Line 7 or 8, because they do not correspond. Line 7 or 8. Line 9, actually. Page 34 anyway, wherever the name of the village occurs. On one screen, it is line 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's page 32, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Line 19 on page 32, and line 8 or 9 on page 34. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes. Mr. Meek, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, today, this morning in your testimony, you used the term "Chetnik" approximately ten or 11 times. Could you please tell me what you mean by a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about that. I'm sorry to actually classify all Serbs, Serbs that were in the Serbian army, as Chetniks. In fact, not all of them were Serbs. Some Serbs underwent the same kind of torture. And a neighbour of mine in Bratunac, whose name I will not mention for reasons of safety, he was a locksmith, a metal worker in the mine. And he was tortured because he helped some people flee to the free territory, gave them shelter. And I know that there were some people in Sarajevo, too, who were Serbs, quite a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Briefly, Judge, could we go into private session, so I could ask this witness one question based on his last answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in -- not yet. We are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, you actually never have described your definition of what you have been calling Chetniks this morning. However, I put it to you that in your answer you apologise and say you are sorry. Sir, is it true that you are sorry because "Chetnik" is a derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I put it? That's a term for people -- well, these are not people at all. It is a monstrous name as far as I am concerned, in light of all that I have been through, and they were the cause. I don't think that real Serbs deserve to be called by this name, because by definition the entire Serb military -- well, not all of them were Chetniks. I mean the ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, earlier on in your testimony at page 23, line 24, in answering a question put to you by the Prosecutor, you answered in regards to leaving Zepa that, "This was forcible transfer of those who had survived from the other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And it is true that this was forcible transfer of the remnants of those people who, in early 1992, had been transported or killed. And these people somehow managed to stay behind, so I'm sure it was forcible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave your statement which you have already told me you have reviewed, that statement was given on the 11th, 12th, 3rd [sic] of March 2002 to the OTP. Do you recall talking to them and telling them about the 25th of July or around the 25th of July, 1995 in Zepa, that there was a planned evacuation for the elderly, children, and certain age of women. Do you remember that, telling them it was a planned evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I said that I remembered the date and that this was an evacuation that was planned by the Chetniks. The cleansing of the remaining areas in Eastern Bosnia, the enclaves in Srebrenica and in Zepa, so this was the Chetnik plan to move these people out, to transfer them forcibly out of these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you never said that in your statement to the OTP though, did you, back in March 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that it had been announced that there would be an evacuation. The UNHCR and the Red Cross, that they would do the evacuation, but this is not something that they did of their own free will. I don't think that the plan was theirs, the plan for this evacuation. It was a plan concocted by the Chetniks to do this forcible evacuation, because they actually dictated the terms to everybody, to UNPROFOR, to UNHCR in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And I will agree that, in fact, you did tell the OTP in 2002 that the evacuation, which had been planned, was planned by UNPROFOR and the United Nations high command for refugees. Sir, would you agree with me that you have no evidence, whatsoever, that this plans was concocted by, as you say, the Chetniks and that that is just pure speculation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no speculation here. You know that all those villages were burnt down. Well, there must be some reports by the Red Cross, by the UNHCR and UNPROFOR about the situation in the enclaves and the circumstances of the fall of the enclave. This is evidence; this is proof. All the villages were burnt, and those people who were left behind in the enclave after the fall, they were all killed. A lot of people were killed. So it was a plan on the part of the Chetniks to kill and to remove all the non-Serb population from the territory of Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, what you have just talked about are -- strike that question. Basically, sir, you still have no evidence other than certain events happened and you believe again you said the Chetniks had this plan. But you don't have any evidence personally, do you, sir? Other than what you are speculating?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question. He has already answered that question. It's the same question phrased differently, but the answer he has given to the previous question answers that question, too. So let's move to the next question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Who is next, Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness because the events in Zepa do not concern our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anybody from the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you testified today about the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica, and the event when your family was unable to leave Srebrenica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993, approximately March or April, the spring. The first convoy -- the first or the second convoy when the trucks with humanitarian aid came in; that's when I was supposed to send my wife and children to Tuzla. But because of the chaos that reined, it was very difficult. People rushed in in panic. I wanted to just leave the -- people wanted to leave the chaos, and I was unable to put my wife and children on that convoy so we went back home. And there was a second attempt before that when it was announced over the media, in the Serbian media in fact, that the corridor would be opened towards Tuzla. I went -- I set off on foot with my wife and children. There were some other families with us, down this road, and I encountered some people who had already taken this so-called corridor, but they had encountered an ambush on that route. Some people were killed, some people fled. Among these people was my brother-in-law. In fact, he was my wife's sister's husband. He -- he was there with his wife. His wife actually came back the first day. He was there for five days with his children. They told us that this was a dangerous route, so we went back to Srebrenica. I think we stayed there until June 1993. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first attempt to leave the enclave was before the Srebenica enclave was established, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, may I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps reason being that you are overlapping, but your question did not show up in the transcript. Mr. Thayer, is that the reason you were up?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you can repeat your question for the purpose of the record; otherwise, we had heard it, but it's not on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to just make a small pause after I make my question so that we can have everything interpreted. So my question was whether this evacuation of your wife and children that you were talking about, whether this happened after the protected area in Srebrenica was already established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that it was already established, the enclave, I mean. But at that time, I think that Morillon arrived, and the first convoy that reached Srebrenica bringing food, that was the occasion. And those were the trucks that I was supposed to put my family on and send them on to Tuzla. So that was April, March, I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the exact date, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in this period, 1993, UN vehicles that brought in humanitarian aid were used to take a total of 7.500 people from the enclave of Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that women and children were taken there, quite a lot of them, but I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this would be the approximate figure for the women, children, and the elderly who went to Tuzla in this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may be so. It may be so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And all of them were taken on UN vehicles in those convoys; in other words, on those trucks and buses to Tuzla; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Tuzla in trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the people who went to Tuzla want to go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody wanted to leave peacefully and in safety because it was not safe to live in Srebrenica, and it also swayed the people, made them leave. And the people from the UNHCR allowed it because there was this humanitarian disaster: No water, no power, no food, no accommodation. This huge mass of people in Srebrenica, about 40, 45.000 people. So it's -- it's a great mass of people for a town that had less people before the war. Even in normal conditions, it would be difficult to handle this mass of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs in the population of Srebrenica before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, until the war, there were Serbs living there; Catholics, too; Muslims. In fact, I really don't have the figures, but of course there were such people. My school mates, my friends, were Serbs. In fact, in -- in that period, I didn't even look at people's names to tell whether they were Serbs, Muslims, Catholics. I really couldn't tell the difference between a Catholic and a Serb, for instance, because until that time we were all the same. We -- in fact, that's how I looked at things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, when the evacuation of the people started, were there any Serbs living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Please take my word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me conclude by asking you this: Did any -- did your acquaintance and your school mate that you were telling us about, did he tell you about -- did he tell you in 1995 that some men from Srebrenica and Zepa actually managed to get to Macedonia and Serbia before these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. In 1994, in early 1995, this is when this happened. A lot of people from Srebrenica, forced by hunger and lack of normal conditions and general uncertainty and lack of safety, they tried to leave the enclave. A man by the name of Harbas was among them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redaction) Macedonia, but this was not true. He never managed to get to Macedonia. He was captured and arrested and detained in Serbia. I don't when he was released, but there were people who actually managed to get to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Stojanovic. We have consulted amongst us, and I think it's safer to redact line -- from line 20 and 21. Just redact the name of the man, and then the next line, the four words in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we did see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me just ask you this: Do you know that the commander of the 28th Division -- that the command of the 28th Division did everything it could to prevent able-bodied men to leave the enclaves of Srebenica and Zepa down this route, leading to Macedonia through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because not too many people left. There was a case, in fact, my brother-in-law or son-in-law wanted to go to Tuzla, but only one person survived out of this group. So they never managed to reach the free territory. He had decided to go to Tuzla though. I don't know about any efforts to prevent people from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just conclude with one question, if we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been agreed, Your Honour, that I should go before Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Josse. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, earlier today, you were asked by the prosecuting counsel about whether you had any contact with those UNPROFOR soldiers; that's at page 7, line 24. And you volunteered the fact that you actually bought petrol from them in order to keep your motor saw going. Did you buy or sell any other goods with UNPROFOR soldiers in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you could call it buying; it was a trade. I have a very nice orchard. My father's orchard in the village, and I made plum brandy, which I exchanged for petrol with the UNPROFOR people. It was barter. Plum brandy for petrol. I didn't sell anything. I mean, I used the petrol for my own personal needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, presumably, some of the other inhabitants of Zepa did the same; in other words, they entered into barters and exchanges with the UNPROFOR troops; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about others. Probably they did, just like I did. I heard from one person that you can exchange petrol for plum brandy, so I would give two litres of plum brandy for five litres of petrol. That was the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other commodity that the UNPROFOR troops were selling or exchanging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the UNPROFOR, but there was a black market or smuggling. I don't know how they -- these goods got there, but we would be selling or -- sugar, coffee, tobacco, salt. I don't know how this got in. I don't think that the UNPROFOR was involved in this. This was outside on the lines with the Serbs. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say you would be "selling," these commodities, were you selling to UNPROFOR or were they selling to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't selling. I brought plum brandy, gave it to them, and it was in exchange for -- it was an exchange, not selling, for petrol, which I used for my own needs at home to cut timber. I was making a small barn for a cow and I was also making a fence, so I used that petrol to power the saw to cut wood. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on. The next matter I want to ask you about is this: You described towards the end of your evidence in chief what your wife had told you about her departure from the enclave. Did she also mention to you that there was an UNPROFOR soldier on each and every bus that departed the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't mention that. She didn't say that there was one, no. She didn't mention it. She didn't say it. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't say that there was an UNPROFOR soldier in the convoy. In her convoy, there were no UNPROFOR soldiers. It was a Chetnik evacuation escorted by the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the inhabitants of the enclave moved down from the hills and mountains in order to leave, did they, as far as you are aware, destroy or damage their own property in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. I know in my own case that it is hard to destroy your own property, your own house, anything of yours; that doesn't make sense. It was all destroyed later by the Chetnik army, plundered and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you that at least some of the destruction was caused by departing Bosniaks, because they didn't want to leave their property to be plundered by Serbs. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that it's absolutely not true. My brother crossed over after two months, and they had been hiding in the woods in the canyon where I had gone to hide. That's where he was. None of them had burned anything. The only chance they had was once it got dark is to go and dig up some potatoes from where they were planted. That was it. As for what was burned, they would see something burning or see what had been burned when the night was over, and they passed by that way the next day. They would see what had been set on fire. As for the property, that was definitely destroyed by the Chetniks, including the house of my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you about is, in fact, your brothers, and perhaps we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the last question I just asked you, Witness, you said you didn't know anything about that agreement. When did you first learn of that agreement, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the first time that I heard about it, through your question. I didn't know about any secret agreements, because we were isolated. We didn't have any access to the media. We didn't get any media reports that would make it possible for me to learn about that. It may have been brought to the attention of the command in Zepa.
