utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you become aware that approximately 800 other men from Zepa had crossed the Drina into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I left the camp, we knew that there was a large number on the basis of the information provided by UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and the Red Cross. And when I came back, in fact, this is the information from the UNHCR and the Red Cross. The report spoke about 950 people; 450 in the camp where I was, and about 500 in the Sljivovica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the fact of the matter is, Witness, that you, in common with those 800 men, were, in fact, instructed via radio lines from Sarajevo to make your way to Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not right. That's ridiculous, as far as I am concerned. What kind of instructions? Well, at that time all I wanted to do was to commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And by the same token, were you not aware that on the 15th of July Rasim Delic had issued an order to defend Zepa with all possible means? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In short, what I'm suggesting to you is that the movement across the Drina was part of an organised military operation, a decision having been made not to engage Serb forces in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I went to Zepa on my own initiative. In fact, I wanted to leave the Zepa enclave and to move to Macedonia via Serbia unnoticed. This idea never occurred to me until I met the school mate of mine who told me that it was possible that we could pass through, that he knew the terrain, that he worked in this company, Partizan Put, in Serbia before the war, that he knew the roads very well, and that we should get to Macedonia where we would be safe and where there would be somebody to take us in. That was what prompted me to leave, to go to Macedonia through Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, earlier on you said that you no longer had water in 1993 in Srebrenica. Is it fair to say that you were not in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, no, I was not, but I was there from June 1992 until approximately June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But with regard to 1995, you cannot say whether there was water-supply or not in Srebrenica, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was water to the same degree that they had it when I was in Srebrenica. There were some makeshift arrangements made for water to be used from the old water-supply system that had been restored to operation, and there were some small springs. They would be -- efforts were made to improve them so that there would be more water from them. But at any rate, there was in the enough water. People had to wait in lines to get some; what I mean to say, is drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But since you were not in Srebrenica in 1995, you could not see that people were queuing for water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there from 1992 and 1993, and I had to stand in those lines and wait for my turn to get water. In 1993 and then -- actually, in early 1993, I felt the shortage of water myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could we agree that with regard to 1995, you knew nothing regarding water-supply in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people who came up to beg for food to the villages, they said that nothing had changed, that the situation was in effect the same. But the UNHCR and the Red Cross, those people said they created a new village in Jadar to relieve the pressure in Srebrenica, moving some people to Jadar. I guess they had some water springs there. I think that the situation was better there when the refugee camp was set up there. I don't know how many people were there, but quite a few of them. And they say -- they said that this village was really very nice, well appointed, and all that. It was in Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you agree to say that the situation improved once you had left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? I didn't understand your question. Well, it did improve for me because I went to the Zepa enclave, to the village there. The humanitarian aid was quite regular. I had my father there, and I had land that I could work. I could raise crops. So in 1994 and 1995, I had my own crops that I could use.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you would also receive humanitarian aid, besides the crops or your produce, besides the food you could produce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, oil, sugar, washing powder, that was mostly it; and clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you do indeed mention in your statements that you took care of distributing humanitarian aid. Could you tell us how it was decided who would benefit and what they would get from the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was distributed. The quantity of goods that was received was then distributed to each of the inhabitants; and in this period when the enclave was established, there were some civilian authorities established there and they decided how the humanitarian aid should be distributed. The quantity of goods that arrived would be divided equally among the inhabitants, so everybody would receive the same -- the same quantity.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it, therefore, fair to say that the people from Zepa and the refugees who took refuge in Zepa would obtain the same quantity of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the place where I was when I distributed the aid, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you would give part of the humanitarian aid to the military unit stationed in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just distributed to the individuals in accordance with the list of residents; nothing was set aside for this or that. The goods were received and then they were distributed to people and you would give it to such-and-such a person; first name, last name. Every person, for instance, would get 3 or 400 grams of sugar. That's how I did it in the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you say that each individual would receive that, that would mean that the members of the military unit would also get the humanitarian aid, as any other residents in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as civilians, but these were in effect civilians. They were people who did not have any uniforms, nothing. That's how aid was distributed. You did not make any distinction. I don't know that anything was set aside for the military, at least not in my place. When the humanitarian aid arrived, we would distribute it on the basis of the number of people that were on the list -- or families, number of families. You knew that if a family had five members, then the humanitarian aid was distributed in accordance with this. So, for instance, if you had one litre of oil, then you would get one litre per person. Well, that was not the case, but I'm just giving you an example. You would have an allocation, allotment of 200 grams per person and that's how I handed it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether the authorities in Zepa - so I mean Zepa, not your village - whether the authorities would collect or would take part of the humanitarian aid for the brigade that was stationed, that had its headquarters in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, because I was not there. I didn't

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we need a redaction. I believe we're in open session, so just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- page 63, line 6, please, and 7, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 63, line 6 and 7, please. Agreed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, previously, you speak about the Zepa Brigade and its premises. Did I understand you correctly when you said that the premises were close to the UNPROFOR premises in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, it was the command. But without any weapons, it was in effect a civilian type of structure. I -- it was like a peacetime command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever go to the premises of the Zepa Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where the premises were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, down-town in the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell me, if you know, what is the distance between the brigade headquarters and the UNPROFOR premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR, I think they were in the elementary school building, and the brigade may have been in the outbuildings. I don't really know the -- the layout of Zepa. I cannot remember it anymore, so I couldn't give you a very specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were speaking about the auxiliary and the outbuildings. Are these buildings that are part of the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it belonged to, but there were some outbuildings there where humanitarian aid was distributed and then there were some other buildings further away. I don't know. I -- I'm now just telling you this from my memory, but I'm not very, very accurate, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Fine. You spoke with a representative of the OTP last week, and you told them that there was a black market in Zepa. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was the -- whatever you want to call it. We call it the smuggling -- we call it smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, you stated that the goods sold on the black market were sold by the Serbs. Did you mean to say that the Serbs themselves would bring those goods to Zepa, would take them to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the routes that those goods took to get to Zepa, but there were some cases. I don't know about dates, but I know that there were such activities going on, smuggling activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you said to the OTP, and this is a statement, prior statement I only have in English. "[In English] There was a black market, but the goods were being sold by Serbs." [Interpretation] I want to know whether the Serbs did, indeed, sell goods in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the goods that arrived in Zepa through the black market, the smuggling activities, they came to Zepa from Serbs, but they didn't go into Zepa to sell it. It was sold by those people who managed to get it illegally from the Serbs by crossing the lines in some way. They managed to get the goods across the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Today, you spoke about the evacuation of Zepa through which your family were evacuated from Zepa. This is what I'm trying to understand: When you abandoned, when you left your family behind in the village where you left them behind before you took the road to Serbia, you did indeed leave your family because you thought they would be safe there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that 99 percent was actually the opposite of my intention to put them somewhere safe, but it was simply not possible to do anything else. I really took it hard, the fact that I had to leave them behind, not knowing what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you said that in 1993, you had an opportunity to let your family go, to let them leave Srebrenica, and you did not take that opportunity because you feared for your children. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In 1993, I was afraid for my -- the lives of my children, if they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, how much more time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five to ten minutes, Mr. President. We could have the break now, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there -- is there going to be a cross-examination by you, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There may be a couple of questions, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break now. 25 minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, just before the break, I asked you a question regarding the evacuation that took place in 1993 [sic], and you told me that you were afraid that the life of your children would be threatened if they left. Now, can we say that in 1993 [sic], when you left your family, before you went to Serbia that you were absolutely certain that they would be evacuated? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a date correction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that he said to Serbia in 1993. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terribly sorry. I meant 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left your family in -- behind in 1995, before you left for Serbia, were you absolutely certain and convinced that your family would be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent I was convinced that they would be evacuated, but I wasn't sure about their safety, 90 percent. The situation was such that I was afraid for their lives, in view of the things that I heard were happening in Srebrenica from people who survived Srebrenica. And in 1992 when there was the public call to the population to go to the stadium, stories about what happened to them, the tortures and so on, I wasn't sure that they would be safe. I was sure about the evacuation because that was the Chetnik desire, to capture the territory without the population, without anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, you constantly talk about Chetniks. Can we say that when you left to Serbia in 1995, that you would never have left your children in the hand of those Chetniks, as you call them, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but the situation was such, it was taking a chance, if you survived or not. I mean I wasn't sure that they would be safe. I thought -- well, I believed that the evacuation would take place with the assistance of the UNHCR and the Red Cross, but I wasn't sure, since everything was under the control of the Chetniks; the UNHCR, the Red Cross, the UNPROFOR, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. But can we agree on the fact that at the time, and I'm talking to you about the day you left your family behind, were you absolutely certain that the international organisations such as the UNPROFOR, the HCR, and other international organisations, that they would be there and present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed that they would be there. Because the UNPROFOR was in Zepa, I assumed that they would have the protection of the UNPROFOR and the international organisations that were helping the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it true to say that you left for Serbia before the beginning of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not true, because I had decided to take the trip to Macedonia through Serbia later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it true to say that when the evacuation started you were not present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I did not dare to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you were not able to see how the evacuation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't dare, because I might have been captured or arrested immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, did you know that some men, able-bodied men, were evacuated through that same convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was in the first convoy. The first convoy was the one

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to redact line 15, please. Please be careful, Witness. This is for your own protection. Avoid mentioning names of relatives and places which are related to you, intimately related to you, while we are in open session. We are going to redact what you said anyway. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, during your testimony, you said that your wife told you that she had to go on foot from Tisce to the territory that was under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but do you know that that portion of the road that belonged, in fact, to no one, that this was a land that wasn't controlled or that was controlled by no one, neither by the Serbs and neither by the Muslims? It was a sort of a no-man's land.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife said that there were Chetniks along the road up until the tunnel. There is a place where there is a tunnel. The Chetniks -- the Chetnik army was there up until the tunnel. From the place where they were disembarked from the buses until the free territory, so up until the Tisce tunnel, the Chetnik army was present. They were asking some people for money, and that's what she said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Upon reflection, we have no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there are no further questions for you, sir, which means your testimony ends here. You will be assisted by our staff. I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish you a very successful completion of your job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just three items, Your Honour, reflected on the tender sheet, which I believe has been distributed to all parties. The first one being under seal, and the next two being different versions of the map shown to the witness, the second of which was marked by him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One question. Let's go to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, for the record, while we were in private session discussing tendering of documents exhibits, on the Prosecution side P02401, P02419, and PIC00061 are being admitted. The first one of these will be the pseudonym sheet. It will be kept under seal, and the Gvero Defence team have tendered 6D24, 6D25, 6D26, and 6D27. They are all being marked for identification, pending translation thereof, upon which they will be admitted fully into evidence. 6D25 will remain under seal. Okay. Do you have the next witness ready? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just before the witness comes in, I'd like to tell the Chamber that I'm very worried by the testimony of the witness, and I want to oppose to the two documents that are supposed to be shown to the Court through this witness. These are P2428 and P2429. There are several documents to be found in these two sets. They were not on the 65 ter list, on the one hand; and on the other hand, these are documents that are obviously from 1993 and 1994, that is outside the time period for the indictment. I am also worried because upon reading the witness's statements as well as the information provided lately by the Prosecution, it appears that most of this testimony will be devoted to the disappearance of the spouse of this witness, and there is no mention in the indictment of any disappearance or any murder. So this is clearly an event that is outside the indictment. Of course, this is a very relevant witness for this case because she lived in Zepa in 1995, but I'd like the part of her testimony devoted to the fate of her husband to be excluded from the testimony; as well as the two exhibits the Prosecution wanted to submit through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Soljan. Let's take them one by one. Let's deal first with the documents to which Madam Fauveau referred; namely, P2428 and P2429. What do you have to say about those?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I respectfully disagree with what the learned counsel says. Indeed, the documents P02428 and 2429 go directly to the issue of intent in this case. As we can see even in the indictment, as the Prosecution has stated, it's starting from paragraph 19, we discuss the six directives, rather, the six strategic objectives that were actually printed out and published in 1992, which very clearly demonstrate the intent to eliminate Drina as a border between Serbia and put Serbia together -- or the Serb nation, Serb people together. And, therefore, it goes directly to the events that therefore occur in both Zepa and Srebrenica in 1995. The correspondent is not only 1993, 1994. There is also correspondence that take place in March of 1995. Again, it goes and very clearly demonstrates, as we intend to show, that this intent that was already enunciated in 1992, in the six strategic objectives, that they continued in directive 7 of in 1995, continues and ends up in the result that we got in the fall of Srebrenica and the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can also further clarify. With respect to the fact that these numbers did not have -- did not have 65 ter or were not on the 65 ter list, we only received these documents from our witness at the end of July of last year. We promptly disclosed them to the Defence a week later, so they have had these documents. This is nothing that's new to the Defence. That's the only reason they did not make it in the 65 ter list. These are documents that represent correspondence between the husband of our witness, Avdo Palic, and various VRS officers, including General Palic, Kusic, and others, directly going to the -- the attempt by the VRS to get the Muslim population out of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to, underscore the fact that we have new documents. We now are being informed that these documents have been received by the Prosecution last summer. Now we'd like to have a ruling from the Trial Chamber whether they can just pick documents like this, without even seeking applying for them to be included on their list. The fact that they gave us those documents this summer is not a reason for us to consider these documents as documents that will be used with witnesses. As a minimum, Mr. President, the Prosecution should make a formal application to add these documents to its list. The Trial Chamber has said what we considered to be a very low threshold standard for any documents to be admitted on the list. We respectfully disagree with that standard that has been sought. We asked for certification of that decision; this has been denied to us. We are operating with this very this low threshold standard. We are now going below again, where we are going to take documents from the Prosecution for which they did not even seek application. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Soljan, on this do you wish -- Mr. Ostojic. Is it on the same score, same ground or not; or are you going to mention something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to mention something else, but it is unrelated on this point, Your Honour. I want to join the motion, the oral motion. But I would like to point to that, Mr. President, on January 25th of this year, specifically on page 49, the Court said something. I want to respectful refresh your recollection, and you said, "There are certain rules that govern our procedure meant to protect the rights of our accused that we would always protect. We feel, quite candidly, that these rules are not only being bent at times, which we understand under certain circumstances that it is coming close to being broken and that the protection of the accused is not being seen, specifically with some of these documents." And this may be a good time to highlight that with this one, I strongly believe that they are being broken, these rules. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really cannot say when the Prosecutor received the documents. The fact of the matter is that the witness's statements date back to April 1999; and during that interview with the OTP, the witness did mention the documents, and I even believe she brought copies of the documents with her. So I think she did speak about those documents; in other words, the Prosecution has been aware of the documents since April of 1999. With regard to the document dated March 1995, no objection whatsoever. However, all the documents dated back to 1993, 1994, I object to them. And I don't want to use too strong terms, but I think it is rather unbelievable that the Prosecutor should tell us now that the indictment covers the period going back to 1992. I thought we believed it was March 1995; and when we asked for Oric exhibit to be disclosed to us, it was the Prosecutor who was against it, very firmly so, saying that there was no connection in time between the two cases. So here I am rather amazed to hear from the Prosecutor that the indictment should start in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I notice Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's -- I would invite counsel to read the indictment. Clearly, we talk about, as Ms. Soljan said, the plan of the Serbs to ethnically divide the state and we cite the key documents, and that's been a part of the background of the indictment. It's the same plan that goes into effect on March when we speak of the 7.1, the famous Karadzic directive. We have chosen to start this case formally with that directive. But clearly as this Court knows, and as this Tribunal knows, this plan and this system to remove the non-Serbs from Bosnia began before that; and began as we've laid out in the background documents, and we have talked about. We are not getting in depth in that. We don't want to go in there. If we started this case in 1992, we would still be in 1992. It is important for the Court to see that. The two documents we are talking about here are letters. There is a letter in 1995 from commander Palic to Kusic, the commander of the Rogatica Brigade, and the response. It is unclear whether there are actual responses to each -- we probably don't have all the correspondence, but they are very similar. And there are very similar letters in 1993 on a similar subject and a with similar kind of tone which you will recognise when you read the letter. It talks about the Serbian state and the salvation of your people, and this kind of thing. Trying to take 1993 out of 1995 in the Bosnian war is absurd. We don't want to get into all the details and go through everything. But when a woman who has had her husband murdered, brings these letters to us, we see the originals. We make a last-minute decision that these things are important. In a perfect world, we would have recognized them earlier and we would have applied to get them on a 65 ter list, but we didn't because we have been in a mad rush to get witnesses here. We got here, we saw this material, and so she will certainly talk about it. And I am sure that once she starts talking about it, you would want the letters themselves. So that's how that has come up. But the absolute -- the relevance of 1993 and the state of mind as it affects 1995, I mean is absolutely crucial. I mean nobody in 1995, as you know, when they decided whether or not to leave their homes, is thinking about on what happened in 1995. They're thinking about the war and the fear and everything else that drove them out. So we don't want to get into detail in all these other years, but some -- some big points, I think you will want to hear from these two letters being -- or this one letter from 1993, it's only one letter in 1993. All the stuff about the investigation or the -- the -- into the murder of her husband is something that we identified to them out of an abundance of caution, but we are not asking her to get into nor are we going to deal with any of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Having addressed two of the issues raised, one is the one raised by Madam Fauveau; namely, that even going back to one of the earliest witness statements, reference was made to these documents, and still it seems that they only came, according to your statement, in the possession of the OTP in August of this year. So question number one arises, why not before? And the second thing is still, if they were available and you attach at least since August of this year and you attach so much importance to them, as related to this witness or maybe even unrelated to witness, why did you choose the procedure of making your intention known to make use of them now without a specific request to have them introduced in the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- the documents I would -- I believe Madam Fauveau, they're mentioned a long time ago. And we've had them since -- since August. In a perfect world, I would recognize all my exhibits and I would get them on a 65 ter list. The fact is until we focused on what she brought with her and what she talked about before, we hadn't made that decision. I have not been able to excruciatingly look in every detail of every witness to determine what might or what might not be a potential exhibit. We have done a pretty darned good job, but we have failed in that respect. It wasn't until Ms. Soljan met with the witness and outlined the testimony that these documents obviously appeared relevant. These documents have been known to the Defence. The witness has been on the Defence list forever, so there is no surprise going on here. The documents, they are not the most critical documents in the world. They give you an idea of what's in the head of one of the brigade commanders, the Rogatica commander, and what Avdo Palic had to deal with as the commander of the Zepa Brigade. They are -- and, in fact, in that regard I think you will be interested in, do they go directly to the key issues of the case. You know, we can live without these documents, but they are the kind of documents that I think would be helpful to the Court. I wish I could have found them and identified them earlier, but we didn't. If that's -- if that's the case, we certainly can live by your decision. But that's the -- that's the situation we find her in. There is no surprise whatsoever here. These have been around for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But given -- one moment, Madam Fauveau. Given -- or just for argument's sake that whatever you are submitting is tenable, still why should we accept a procedure whereby you come here to court and make it known that you plan to use these two documents with this witness and not seek permission to include them in the 65 ter list in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should have been done, and I don't think you should accept that procedure. And I -- I stand at fault for that, Your Honour. I did not -- did not realise that was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am more and more worried, because frankly here I see no relevance whatsoever as to know what was in the head of one of the commanders of one of the Rogatica units, which has no link at all with one of the accused. There is no subordination relationship with any of the accused. Now, how can the intent of somebody who is not on trial here, how can that be of any relevance of this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I understand was in relation to the Zepa group unit. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this -- these submission have expanded slightly, could I add this observation, which is as follows: With respect, without teaching my grandmother to suck eggs, we would contend this Trial Chamber needs to try and keep this case within as narrow confines as possible. And if this sort of evidence is admitted, it would, to some extent, at least allow the Defence, when our turn comes, to introduce evidence to counter for example what was in the witness's head and to try and counter-explain it. If it's good for the goose, it's good for the gander, excuse me, twice using very colloquial expressions. Perhaps it is the best way I can express my point. We would urge the Court to keep the case within as narrow confines as possible, because otherwise the Defence will be allowed surely to answer things which run counter to the defendants' interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, while Madam Usher will prepare the witness to come in for the few minutes that are left, our position is as follows: I think we have made it clear that barring some exceptional circumstances when it happens that a witness will just take out of his or her pocket a document, much to everybody's surprise, the procedure that we have established; namely, that you should seek permission to have the documents included in the 65 ter list before they are made use of, they are made use during testimony or put to a witness, should be followed. So we won't start with the testimony of this witness without having first decided on this matter, and you are asked to file a proper motion today. And, tomorrow, we will give the opportunities to parties to make further submissions if it is the case, and then we will decide, we will hand down our decision and proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, please make yourself comfortable. By the way, this witness has no protective measures, no? No. No protective measures. Madam, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have kept you waiting, but there is a procedural issue that has to be determined before you start giving evidence. I wanted to apologise to you. We will start with your evidence tomorrow morning, after we have decided on this matter. In the meantime, perhaps you can be sworn in. Please stand up. That is the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make before you start giving evidence. Could you read it out aloud, please, and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Madam, please make yourself comfortable. You will return again tomorrow morning, as I said, Ms. Palic, and we will take it up from there. Thank you. In the meantime, even though you haven't really started testifying as such, you are requested not to discuss with anyone or let anyone discuss with you the subject matter of your testimony. She has been sworn in. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We thank you, and we will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you. So, I think we have to leave it at that. I wouldn't like to keep the next Trial Chamber waiting unduly. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
